findings.where: explain.text (Book), end of the kelvin paragraph
findings.what: "Every watt a motor draws has to go somewhere as energy each second. The pump puzzle needs that bookkeeping." points at a puzzle that is not in this lesson and talks about what comes later; cut both sentences, or keep only the plain point that a joule each second is a watt, which is already made in the cooler example.

The explanation carries eight footnote markers ([^4], [^2] and [^5] twice each, one on each sentence of the bold takeaway, one on the general sentence that energy depends on mass, material and rise), more than a few and not on values he would look up; keep [^1] on 4,200, [^2] once on 334 and 2,260, and [^3] on 3,850, and drop the rest.

"Temperature follows how fast the molecules jiggle. Melting spends the energy on loosening their hold..." is stated as fact here, but no source carries it and the explanation labels it "one way to picture it"; give the Why the same label.

Each puzzle comes after the screen that gives its answer: screen 4 says the line stays flat for 334 kJ, then screen 5 asks the reading after 200 kJ, so he never commits to the 'energy in means hotter' idea before seeing the flat line, which the brief's section 3 promised; asking the 200 kJ question first, with the thermometer reading '?' and the red wrong-pick lines as the test, would make it a real prediction.
The text runs 92 words, at the 90-word limit; cutting "The two are not the same thing." brings it to 86 without losing the point.

The heater power slider appears with no sentence saying what it does: it changes only the heater time, not the curve. One short sentence such as "The heater's power only sets how long it takes" would make the point that energy, not time, sets the temperature.

findings.where: Curve picture, top row at 360 px (light and dark)
findings.what: The beaker's "steam" label sits almost on the same line as the bar title "Where the energy went" and runs straight into it, so it reads as "steam Where the energy went"; move the steam label down or the bar title along.

The rule under the picture reads "heat each second = kg × 3,850 × rise" when it means kg each second, and the task's "Seawater takes about 3,850 J per kg per °C" is clearer as "Seawater's specific heat capacity is about 3,850 J per kg per °C".

The standing caption "Melting and boiling take in energy at a steady temperature" sits under the puzzles on screens 5, 9 and 13 and gives away their answers; the Finish panel already says it, so the caption could go.

The brief's mapping cites Unit 8's thermal efficiency of a heat transfer process from flow rate, temperature change and input power, but the lesson stops at 'with no losses'; one line, such as heat taken up ÷ power put in, would cover it without re-teaching efficiency from Mechanics and materials.
